This explains "immeasurable light. "Immeasurable" refers to the vast extent of the light that shines upon the ten directions.
It is only the Buddha Amitābha whose light illuminates thousands of myriads of worlds without end, and without any obstruction.

Although the sun and moon possess light, they are obscured by clouds; yet the light of that Buddha penetrates mountains and passes through walls, reaching into the most remote and dark places, all without obstruction. Someone may ask: "That the sun and moon are obstructed is known by everyone."

Question: How can it be known that the Buddha’s light is unimpeded? Answer: Long ago, during the time of Śākyamuni Buddha, there was an old woman in the eastern part of the city who did not wish to see the Buddha and retreated into her inner chambers.
Yet the Buddha’s light shone upon her, penetrating even through the walls so that light filled all directions both inside and outside; this is the very proof that there is no obstruction.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the lifespan of that Buddha, as well as that of his people, lasts for immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
therefore, he is named Amitābha.

This explains that his lifespan is immeasurable. Regarding the lifespan of that Buddha, there are three aspects. First is the lifespan of the *dharmakāya*; it takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its life-force.
Second is the lifespan of the *saṃbhogakāya*; it takes wisdom (*prajñā*) as its life-force. Third is the lifespan of the *nirmāṇakāya*;

it takes causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) as its life-force. The *Fahua shouliang shu* (Commentary on the Lifespan Chapter of the Lotus Sūtra) states: "Regarding these three lifespans, 'lifespan' (*āyus*) refers to receiving..."

Furthermore, as for the Dharma-body, because True Suchness is not separated from all phenomena, it is called "receiving. As for the Reward-body, because object and wisdom are in correspondence, it is called "receiving.
As for the Response-body, because its lifespan is obtained through retribution for a single period and continues uninterrupted for eternal years, it is called "receiving.
Therefore, the life-span of that Buddha is immeasurable, such that no one can exhaustively fathom it. And as for those people...
As for "the people," this does not refer to the inhabitants of this shore. Rather, all these are the inhabitants of the other shore.

Relying upon both the Buddha’s power and their own strength, they single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name. At the time of death, they are reborn on the other shore by transformation within a lotus flower.
This is a body of pure emptiness, not like the obstructed physical body of an ordinary person. Therefore, the inhabitants of the other shore—once [reborn]...
Ascending to the stage of non-retrogression and receiving the mandate upon the [ten] stages is likewise immeasurable and boundless.
As for "asamkhyeya kalpas," it means that one's lifespan is incalculable; as it doubles and doubles again, it is therefore called immeasurable and boundless.
Speaking in truth, the inherent nature is numinous clarity and pervasive penetration—this is the meaning of an immeasurable lifespan. Only then does one truly know Amitābha.
Although the Buddha is beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of buddha-lands, he is in truth seated cross-legged, majestic and unmoving, within the hearts of sentient beings in this Sahā world.
Alas, the beings on this shore often enter the gates of external paths; they needlessly exhaust their own spirits, turning the brilliance of the radiant sun into darkness.
Śāriputra, it has been ten kalpas since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood.
Since you already know the meaning of that Buddha’s name, I wonder at what time he attained Buddhahood. *Kalpa* is a Sanskrit term, also called *kalpā*;
this is translated as "ten parts. Ten *kalpas* are also called *mahā-kalpas* (great kalpas) or *antara-kalpas* (small kalpas).

*Kalpa*. What is now referred to as "a long time" should be understood as a *mahākalpa* (great kalpa). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that each of the four phases—formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness—consists of twenty small *kalpas*.
Thus, eighty small *kalpas* constitute one great *kalpa*. When it speaks of ten great *kalpas*, it refers to these [units of] eighty small *kalpas*.
This explanation is also a discourse delivered according to the capacities of sentient beings for a specific occasion; however, speaking from the ultimate perspective, Ā...
Since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood, it has also been immeasurably immeasurable eons.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that Buddha has immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are arhats;
they cannot be known by means of calculation.
These are the disciples of the Śākyamuni. As for the "immeasurable śrāvakas," they are called śrāvakas because they hear the teaching of the Four Noble Truths and awaken to the Path.
The Four Noble Truths are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. "All are arhats" distinguishes them from those who have attained only the first three fruits of the path.
The term "pratyekabuddha" is not mentioned, as they are subsumed within the category of śrāvakas. They are not something that can be known through mere calculation.
As stated in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the "Chapter on Incalculable Kalpas": "Because it is beyond the reach of the mental power of worldly people, it is simply called 'immeasurable.
The assembly of bodhisattvas is likewise so. Śāriputra, that buddha-land has accomplished such merit."
"Adornment of Virtue.

This explains that the assembly of bodhisattvas is likewise immeasurable. Furthermore, it concludes the preceding section on the primary retributive adornments of the Buddha, the śrāvakas, and the bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, all those beings born in the land of Ultimate Bliss are non-retrogressive (avaivartika).
Among them, there are many who are in their last birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), so numerous that they cannot be known by calculation;
they can only be described as immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya).
"Beings who are born" refers to those beings born in that land who receive benefits in immeasurable numbers.

"Avivartika" (阿鞞跋致) is translated here as "non-retrogressive. Furthermore, fearing that people might doubt whether that land contains many worthies and sages—all of whom have long cultivated themselves in the higher realm and are all non-retrogressive—and whether those newly born there are necessarily non-retrogressive, it is therefore said:
Regardless of whether they are noble ones or ordinary beings, all who attain rebirth there are non-retrogressive; this is to resolve their doubts.
Among them, many are those who will attain Buddhahood in one more life (*ekajātipratibaddha*); even those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) are called "in their final body.

This means they shall become Buddhas in their next life as a "successor" (*upapadya*), not that the title "successor" refers exclusively to attaining Buddhahood in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. One may also be a successor in other worlds.

This refers, for example, to Maitreya Bodhisattva, who is currently in the position of the successor in the Sahā world. Regarding the term "asaṃkhyeya" (incalculable), it has been explained clearly in the preceding text.
[The section on] the adornment of the primary retribution is now complete.
Śāriputra, those sentient beings who hear this should make a vow, vowing to be born in that land.

This is an exhortation for those first developing the aspiration to be reborn in the Pure Land. Śāriputra, for those sentient beings who hear this, the initial exhortation is to develop the aspiration;
the benefit lies in being reborn through the upholding of the Name. Therefore, one hears first and then believes; faith is able to give rise to the aspiration. Faith and aspiration—

Both [faith and practice] are fully prepared; there is no aspect of conduct that is not perfected. That is to say, the three—faith, aspiration, and practice—which are the provisions for the Pure Land, are complete and lacking nothing.
One will certainly attain rebirth there.
Why is this? It is because one has been able to assemble together in one place with such superior and virtuous people.
By "superior and virtuous people," one refers to the aforementioned immeasurable śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and non-retrogressive beings.
"Śāriputra, one cannot be born in that land through a small root of goodness, merit, or causal conditions.

This statement is intended to manifest the superiority of the merit of upholding the Name; by saying that with "small goodness" or "small merit" one cannot attain rebirth, it serves as a prelude to the following passage, which states that by upholding the Name one immediately attains rebirth, thereby highlighting the unique excellence of this merit. The scribe [of the sutra]...
This is because upholding the Name possesses manifold roots of goodness and merit. Yunqi also said: "It is the best among all that is good, and the greatest among all blessings.

Although there is no explicit text to this effect in the sutra, if one observes the passage below stating that by "upholding the Name" one immediately attains rebirth in the Pure Land, and correlates it with the preceding passage stating that those with "few roots of goodness and little merit" cannot attain rebirth, then it follows that even such a person can indeed attain rebirth; thus, its merit and goodness are [immeasurable].
This can be understood. Yet, it is actually because of upholding the Name that one attains such merit; thus, one should accept that upholding the Name itself constitutes great merit.
This is also consistent with the meaning of the sūtras. Now, regarding this one-fascicle *Amitābha Sūtra*, I, Śākyamuni Tathāgata—

There is indeed a profound meaning [to this]. Fearing that ordinary sentient beings, upon hearing these teachings on rebirth in the Pure Land, might doubt that their own roots of goodness and merit are insufficient to provide the causal conditions for rebirth, they would consequently lack firm faith and earnest mindfulness.
At times they would harbor thoughts of regression, and in every moment they would lack the intent to uphold the Name. One must know that while they may have faith...
One must receive this with a single-minded resolve. To hold the Name is itself the root of goodness and the causal condition for merit.
It should be understood that the beings of that land cannot be reborn there by means of meager goodness or meager merit;

rather, by holding the Name and relying upon both the Buddha’s power and one’s own strength, one immediately attains rebirth. Fearing that there may be those of deep faith, it is unnecessary to seek out other roots of goodness or merit.

[The Master] replied: "Simply recite the Buddha's name with single-minded devotion; there is no need to seek anything else. To seek elsewhere is feared to lead one into the ways of external paths (*tīrthika*).
This teaching is intended to cause those who practice the Pure Land method to cease their doubts of regression and give rise to resolute faith.
Therefore, the subsequent passage encourages them by means of upholding the Name. Nevertheless, the practice of holding the Name truly possesses immeasurable roots of goodness."
By virtue of these causes and conditions for merit, Amitābha Buddha accomplished immeasurable vows and practices, as well as immeasurable virtues, during the causal stage;

thus he was able to achieve the sacred title of "Amitābha Buddha. Just as a *dhāraṇī* gate can maintain all phenomena in their entirety, so too this name of Amitābha Buddha can maintain the immeasurable [virtues].

By virtue of this merit, those who are able to uphold the Name—that is, those who recite the name of Amitābha Buddha—possess inconceivable merit fully perfected within a single thought-moment; it is not merely a matter of many roots of goodness and blessings.
Those who can uphold the Name will, without exception, be reborn through mindfulness and enter the stage of non-retrogression.
Śāriputra, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha,
hold fast to his name— whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days—
with single-mindedness and without distraction.
"One-mindedness without distraction" does not mean that one attains non-distraction after one day up to seven days. It is through these seven days that the mind becomes undistracted.
"Without distraction" means holding the name with single-mindedness; during the interval of those seven days, there are no other thoughts or intermingled杂念 (interlaced thoughts).
Furthermore, single-mindedness has two meanings: the mindfulness of phenomena (事念) and the mindfulness of principle (理念). As for the mindfulness of phenomena:
Single-mindedly hold the name and recollect that Buddha, with every thought-moment uninterrupted. Regarding the contemplation of mind:
realize that the mind which recollects is fundamentally empty; understand that the Buddha who is recollected has no substantial body.

Originally pure and transcendentally manifest as the true and eternal, then mountains, rivers, and the great earth are entirely the manifestation of Amitābha; every step one takes is none other than the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
When that person approaches the end of life, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy ones, will appear before them.

"That person" refers to one who practices mindfulness of the Buddha; provided they can maintain single-mindedness without distraction until the moment of death, the Buddha and the holy assembly will manifest before them.
This occurs through the convergence of the Buddha’s power and their own power, responding to one another.

Therefore, the Buddha appears before them. As for those whose karmic consciousness is vast and indistinct, at the time of death, their karmic consciousness naturally manifests before them, and they undergo rebirth according to their karma;
for those who have committed the ten evil deeds or the five grave offenses, the hells manifest before them.

For those who are stingy, greedy, and envious, hungry ghosts appear before them; for those who observe the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, the karmic rewards of humans and devas appear before them.
Now, if one recites the Buddha’s name with single-mindedness and without distraction, pure mindfulness will be accomplished. When facing death, how could the Buddha not appear before one?
Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If one remembers the Buddha and recites his name, in the present and in the future, one will certainly achieve [success]."
This refers to the Buddha.
When such a person reaches the end of their life, their mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.

The previous mention of "approaching" (lin) meant when one is about to pass away; the present mention of "the time of death" (zhongshi) means that the eight consciousnesses have ceased their activity. As for the eight consciousnesses:
This refers precisely to the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*), also called the *gandharva* body. This consciousness serves as the vanguard when coming and the last to depart;
it is this very consciousness that takes birth according to karma. Regarding "the mind not being inverted": because the mind is undistracted, it is not inverted;
because it is not inverted, one is not reborn in other realms, but attains rebirth [in the Pure Land]. Thus it is said.

As for its swiftness: "inversion" refers to the fact that because one has habitually followed along with deluded thoughts and engaged in karmic actions throughout one's life, failing to cultivate right mindfulness, the mind becomes largely distracted. Consequently, at the time of death, all the evil karma previously created manifests before one.
Thus, the things one had accomplished in the past all come forth simultaneously in an instant; this is what is meant by inversion. Such is this inversion.
Inverted and submerged within the cycle of rebirth across the six realms, one changes head and face, taking birth according to one's karma.
Now that you are single-mindedly undistracted—concentrating right mindfulness within and invoking Amitābha without—you will be welcomed into the Lotus Land.
Shedding this ordinary human body, you shall cast yourself into a lotus womb as a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya), thereby ascending directly to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Śāriputra, it is because I see this benefit that I speak these words: if there are sentient beings who hear this teaching, they should make a vow to be born in that land.

"This benefit" refers to the aforementioned vision of the Buddha and rebirth there. This statement, "I see this great benefit," is why he speaks the words of single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha. It is because once one has attained rebirth, it is called self-benefit;

having been born in that land, hearing the Dharma and attaining the fruit, and subsequently extensively delivering sentient beings, is called benefiting others. Possessing these two benefits is what is meant.
Sentient beings who hear this should make a vow to be reborn in that land. If one does not vow to be reborn there, they will have failed the Buddha’s teaching. This is the second exhortation.
Śāriputra, just as I now praise the inconceivable benefits of the meritorious virtues of Amitābha Buddha, so too does this Śākyamuni Buddha personally and clearly praise them,
desiring to reveal and manifest that the Buddhas of the six directions likewise offer praise in the following text.
"Extol" (*praśaṃsā*) means to praise. "Exclaim" (*udāna*) means to utter a sigh of emotion. To extol and glorify the vast merits of that Buddha causes people to take refuge with faith.
To be moved by emotion and sigh deeply regarding this Dharma—so rare among gods and humans and so difficult to encounter throughout kalpas—causes people to feel both sorrow and joy.
Joy arises from having heard it; sorrow arises from lamenting that one has heard it too late.
Regarding the benefits of inconceivable merit, the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states:

"This mind, from its very origin, is free from the characteristics of mental objects and free from the characteristics of verbal expression; therefore, to raise the mind is immediately an error, and to stir a thought is immediately a deviation."
Those who cling to words are deluded; those who merely receive the teachings lose [the truth]. Yet, what should one do?

Even if one were to seal the mouth and forget all mental activity, one would still fall into the state of non-discrimination (*avyākṛta*). Non-discrimination refers to that which is neither good nor evil.
If a person can believe in such a matter, you should know that this person possesses the benefit of inconceivable merit.
In the eastern direction, there are also Buddhas such as Akṣobhya Buddha, Merudhvaja Buddha, Mahāmeru Buddha,
Meruprabhāsa Buddha, and Gadgadasvara Buddha— Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
The names of the Buddhas all possess immeasurable merit and virtue, making them difficult to explain exhaustively.

For now, I shall briefly explain them by way of their causes and effects, natures and characteristics, merits, wisdom, practices, and vows. *Akṣobhya* means "Immovable," because he eternally abides in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
*Sumerukūṭa* means "Peak of Mount Sumeru," because the Buddha’s marks are inexhaustible like Mount Sumeru. As for Mount Sumeru...

This is called "Wondrously High" (*Sumeru*). It is called "wondrous" because it is composed of various jewels; it is called "high" because it rises far above all other mountains. Regarding "wondrous sound":
the Dharma-sound is perfectly wondrous, for the preaching of the Dharma accords with the capacities of sentient beings.

Thus, it is said that the Buddha can expound the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their own kind. Such examples are too numerous to list in full; here, only five have been cited.
The Buddha explained this through an analogy. "Ganges" (恒沙) is also called the *Gaṅgā* River. "Sand" (*śa*) is a metaphor for "abundance.

The Ganges is located in the Western Regions, beside the Lake of No Heat (*Anavatapta*). Atop the summit of Mount Gandhamādana lies the Lake of No Heat and Affliction (*Anavatapta*), from which four rivers flow.
The Ganges flows to the south; it is forty *li* wide, and its sand is carried by the current, being the finest of all. The Buddha...

He preached the Dharma near that river. Whenever he speaks of "many," he frequently takes it as a metaphor; for instance, the many Buddhas in the eastern direction are as numerous as all the grains of sand in the Ganges River.
Each, within their own land, extended their broad and long tongues, completely covering the trichiliocosm,
and spoke these words of truth: "You sentient beings, you should believe this Sūtra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit,
which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas."
"Each in their own country" means each in their respective native land. Regarding the manifestation of the mark of the broad and long tongue:

this is because throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Tathāgata’s verbal karma has been pure; he has refrained from false speech and frivolous talk, and has avoided harsh words and double-tongued speech.
Because he constantly speaks words that are true, upright, and harmonious, he has brought forth this mark of the long tongue, which is free from falsehood.

Therefore, its breadth is described in terms of the horizontal, while its length is explained in terms of the vertical. Its texture is supple; when the long tongue is extended, it covers the face and reaches up to the hairline.
With its entire broad and long tongue, it completely covers [the body] in a way that is difficult to measure. When he utters a sound, it vibrates everywhere like thunder and is heard universally.
Furthermore, his voice is exceedingly subtle and wondrous, penetrating the Dharma-realm from afar. Someone may ask: "What of the Buddha’s sixteen-foot golden body?"
"How can this physical body possess a tongue-mark that covers the entire trichiliocosm? He replied:
"The sixteen-foot body is the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) for preaching the Dharma to those of the Two Vehicles and ordinary beings.
You should know that the Tathāgata’s pure *dharmakāya* fills the *dharmadhātu* and pervades the ten directions; how could it merely cover the trichiliocosm? Now..."
A "great thousand" (trisāhasra) refers merely to the realm converted by a single Buddha.

A "trichiliocosm" (trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu) consists of four great continents, one sun and moon, one Mount Sumeru, one desire realm (kāmadhātu), one form realm (rūpadhātu), and one formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
This constitutes a single world-system. When the number of these world-systems reaches one thousand, it is called a small chiliocosm.
A thousand times this small chiliocosm is called a medium chiliocosm. A thousand times this medium chiliocosm is called a great trichiliocosm.
All of these undergo the phases of formation, subsistence, destruction, and emptiness; that is to say, ten trillion sets of four continents collectively constitute [a great trichiliocosm].
It is the land of a single Buddha alone. Regarding those who speak words of truth, they must certainly believe that from the tip of a broad and long tongue issues forth truthful speech;
that is to say, you should faithfully believe this *Sūtra on the Merits of Inconceivable Praise, Protected and Mindful of by All Buddhas*, and do not harbor any doubt.
As for "faith," when faith is sincere it is true, and when it is earnest it is real.

Thus, holding the Name with a single mind is not in vain. These sixteen characters—“The Sutra on the Inconceivable Merit of Praise, Protected and Mindfully Kept by All Buddhas”—are the original title of the present sutra. For this reason, while the preceding passage praised the Buddha, the present passage praises the sutra;
their meaning is one and the same. As for the "Sutra Protected and Mindfully Kept," it refers to those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha. The Buddha...

May they be protected by power, granted peace and security, and freed from all obstacles and difficulties. May the Buddha hold them in his heart, inspiring them to diligence so that they do not fall back.
One should know that when one recollects the Buddha and the Buddha recollects one, the response occurs spontaneously; this faith cannot be denied.
Śāriputra, in the world-systems of the southern direction, there are Buddhas such as Candrasūryapradīpa Buddha, Yaśaḥprabha Buddha, Mahājvālāṃsa Buddha,
Merupradīpa Buddha, and Anantavīrya Buddha— Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
As for the Buddha Sūryacandrapradīpa, his great wisdom is inexhaustible, for he is able to shatter the darkness of sentient beings.
Therefore, the sunlight carries the meaning of *prajñā*, while the moonlight that illuminates the night and brings coolness carries the meaning of *vimukti*.

For this reason, he is named the Lamp of the Knowledge of the Paths (*mārgajñatā*). Just as the sun and moon pervade both day and night, abiding in neither extreme, they represent the supreme Middle Way.
Truth. There is the meaning of the Dharma-body; this is called the inexhaustibility of great wisdom.

As for the Buddha Renowned Light (Yaśaḥprabha), his fame is universally heard, like light shining afar, heard throughout immeasurable worlds; wherever the sun’s rays shine, there is nowhere they do not reach.

As for the Buddha Great Flame Shoulder (Mahārciskandha), the shoulders represent the two wisdoms, and the flame is a metaphor for illumination. The two wisdoms are: expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*)... [and] true wisdom (*jñāna*).

The wisdom that illuminates phenomena (sho-ji) is the ultimate wisdom (jissai-chi) that illuminates principle (ri). Phenomena and principle are thus vividly manifest, and the dual illumination is unobscured, like flames erupting from both shoulders.
These two wisdoms are able to bear the burden of all sentient beings toward rebirth in the Pure Land; therefore, they possess the significance of "shoulders."
As for the Buddha Sumerudīpa, his lamp of wisdom is like Mount Sumeru. As for the Buddha Anantavīrya, he has practiced diligence without ceasing throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Each, within their own land, extends the mark of the broad and long tongue, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and speaks words of truth:
"You sentient beings, you should believe in this Sutra on the Merit of Inconceivable Praise, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
Śāriputra, in the western world, there is the Buddha Amitāyus and the Buddha Amitābha.
The Buddha Immeasurable Banner, the Buddha Great Radiance, the Buddha Great Clarity, the Buddha Jewel Mark, the Buddha Pure Light,
and other Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Regarding the Buddha of Immeasurable Life (*Amitāyus*), there are two explanations as he shares the same name as the Original Buddha (*mūlabuddha*); each possesses its own logic. As for these two views:

Lingzhi (Zhixu) maintains that while many Buddhas share the same names, this one must certainly not be the Buddha accomplished by the Bhikṣu Dharmākara, because the Original Buddha would not praise himself. Cien (Xuanzang) states that even if it were a case of self-praise, the principle...
There is no harm in that either; however, Yunqi [Zhuhong] considered it unnecessary to preserve both versions. Now, taking the Buddhas with identical names as the basis is correct.
Regarding Buddhas with identical names, setting aside other sutras, within these six directions there are three Buddhas named Jvalaṃdhara (Flame-Shoulder).
One cannot explain [the term] "self-praise" by means of it; therefore, explaining it through "same-name" (samānanāma) renders its principle broad.
Although explaining it as "self-praise" simplifies ordinary sentiment, its principle is conversely narrow. One should follow Lingzhi:

an "Infinite-Phase Buddha" (Amitābha) is so called because his marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are inexhaustible—whether they be the thirty-two marks, eighty-four thousand marks, or marks as numerous as motes of dust.

Their merit is immeasurable, and their marks are likewise immeasurable. In the past, when Master Zhigong manifested the form of the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara, the monk Zhaoyou was unable to lift his brush;
how much more so for the marks of a Buddha? As for the Buddha Immeasurable Banner (*Amitadhvaja*), his merit is as lofty and manifest as a banner because it is immeasurable.
As for the Buddha Great Radiance (*Mahāprabha*), he possesses vast and great radiance.
"Light" means that its radiance shines far and wide. From the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven upward, the various devas also possess bodily light and do not rely on the sun or moon.
Like those of the Two Vehicles who have attained minor fruits and the Bodhisattvas on the causal stages, all possess radiance; yet compared to the Buddha, theirs is small.
Because the Buddha’s light outshines and eclipses all others, it is called "great. Regarding the "Greatly Enlightened Buddha," it refers to the Buddha by virtue of his greatness...
*Jñāna* (Wisdom): Because it exhaustively destroys all delusions. *Sarvajñā* (All-Knowledge) exhaustively destroys the delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
*Mārgajñatā* (Path-Knowledge) exhaustively destroys the delusions as numerous as grains of sand. *Sarvākārajñatā* (Omnimodal Knowledge) exhaustively destroys the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*).

It is like the bright sun in the sky, which shines everywhere; therefore, it is called "Great Illumination. As for the Buddha of Precious Marks (*Ratnākara*), his marks and signs are exceptionally sublime, as precious and noble as jewels.
Therefore, as for the Buddha Pure Light (Vimalaprabha): because the Buddha’s virtues are pure, he emits radiance. Regarding "pure emission of light":
wisdom that is subject to defilement does not emit sublime light; it is because the Buddha’s virtues are supremely pure that he emits great radiance.
Each, in their own land, extends a broad and long tongue that completely covers the trichiliocosm and speaks words of truth:
"You sentient beings, you should believe this Sūtra on the Merit of Inconceivable Praise, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
Śāriputra, in the northern world, there is the Buddha Flame-Shoulder, the Buddha Most Victorious Sound, and the Buddha Difficult...
Dharmadatta Buddha, Sūryagarbha Buddha, Jālinīprabha Buddha, and others such as these—Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

As for Flame-Shoulder (Jvalāṃsa) Buddha, his explanation was provided previously in the section on the southern direction. Regarding Supreme-Voice (Varaghoṣa) Buddha, the Buddha’s voice is subtle and wondrous;
no other sound can equal it. Regarding Unstoppable (Durvighāta) Buddha, the Buddha’s virtues are firm and dense, and cannot be obstructed.
"Because it is indestructible. *Ju* (沮) is a name for water. The Buddha has realized the Dharma-body and has already attained a vajra-like, indestructible essence;

since there are no further delusions, the turbulent flow of afflictions (*kleśa*) can no longer overwhelm him. Thus, it is said to be "difficult to obstruct. Regarding the phrase "the Buddha born from the sun": [it refers to...]

The Buddha’s light appeared like the sun rising in the east. As for the Buddha Net-Light (Jālinīprabha), his wisdom-light was like a precious net, universally covering all sentient beings and illuminating everything without exception.
Each, within their own land, extended the mark of the broad and long tongue, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and spoke these words of truth:
"You sentient beings, you should believe this Sūtra on the Merit of Inconceivable Praise, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
Śāriputra, in the world-system below, there is the Buddha Siṃha, the Buddha Yaśas, and the Buddha Nāmaprabha.
Buddha; Dharmabuddha; Dharmadhvaja Buddha; Dharmadhara Buddha; and other Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
As for Siṃhabuddha (Lion Buddha), he is like a lion, the king among beasts; when it lets out a single roar, all other animals are struck with fear.
Likewise, when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, all non-Buddhists are filled with faith and submission. As for Yaśobuddha (Renowned Buddha), the explanation of the meaning is the same as before.
The Buddha named Kīrtiprabha (Light of Fame) is so called because his name is like the light of the sun, reaching everywhere without exception;
he is like Amitābha Buddha, whose radiance universally illumines the worlds of the ten directions without obstruction.

The Buddha named Dharma is translated here as "Dharma," for by means of the Dharma’s guidance and sustenance, he causes sentient beings to single-mindedly recollect the Buddha and realize the Dharmakāya. The Buddha named Dharmadhvaja (Dharma Banner) is [so called because] the Dharma...
Like a banner, the Buddha-dharma is lofty and manifest; humans and devas look up to it as their guiding principle, while those of wrong views and non-Buddhists submit upon beholding it.

This is identical in meaning to the "Immeasurable Banner" mentioned in the preceding text. As for the Buddha Who Sustains the Dharma, he upholds the Buddha-dharma, falling neither into the extreme of existence nor into the extreme of non-existence, skillfully maintaining the Middle Way. He causes the subtle Dharma to flow freely through the world, so that [beings] may not...
Because it is severed [from delusion], these hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all return to the single square inch of the mind.
Their boundless utility is entirely contained within the source of the mind. If sought, they are without marks or form; if released, they are inexhaustible and endless.
They are originally complete and require no seeking from others. Therefore, when the minds of sentient beings skillfully uphold the meaning of the Middle Way, this is the Tathāgatagarbha.
Furthermore, each of them, within their own lands, extends the mark of the broad and long tongue, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and speaks words of truth:
"You sentient beings, you should believe this praise of inconceivable merit. All Buddhas..."

The *Sūtra on What is Protected and Mindfully Kept*. Śāriputra, in the world-system above, there are the Buddhas Brahma-voice, Constellation King, Fragrant Excellence, Fragrant Light, Great Flame Shoulder, Adorned Body with Variegated Jewel Flowers, and King of the Śāla Trees.
Buddha Ratnakusumaguṇa, Buddha Sarvārthadarśin, Buddha Merukalpa, and other Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—
including Buddha Brahmaghoṣa,
whose speech is pure and who possesses the marks of perfected brahmacarya, and is therefore named Brahmaghoṣa.

Regarding the Buddha *Dhruvarāja* (宿王佛): the moon is the king of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). Ten thousand points of starlight are not equal to the solitary moon; the moon is of a different category than the stars.
This is a metaphor for the Buddha as the Great Awakened One (*mahābuddha*); awakening is of a different category than delusion. Because he surpasses all, he is the king among the lunar mansions.

Regarding the Buddha Fragrance-Supreme: the Buddha is the most holy among the holy, just as this incense is the finest among fragrances. When this incense is burned once, there is no one within forty *li* who does not smell it;

this incense is the supreme fragrance. It is the fragrance of the realization of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*), whose scent universally permeates immeasurable worlds, reaching all humans, devas, asuras, non-Buddhists, and those of the two vehicles.
Its fragrance is such that none can equal it; therefore, he is named "Supreme Fragrance" (Gandhottama). As for the Buddha "Fragrant Light" (Gandhaprabha), his fragrance emits light;
because this fragrant radiance can destroy evil existence and eliminate impurity, and because all evils and defilements are utterly extinguished, he is named "Fragrant Light.

As for the Buddha "Great Flame Shoulder" (Mahārciskandha), this explains the clarity within the southern quarter. As for the Buddha "Adorned with Bodies of Various-Colored Jewel Flowers" (Vicitravarṇaratnapuṣpavyūhakāya), "various colors" refers to...

The teachings of other vehicles are considered defiled and mixed. Now, the Buddha Adorned with Precious Flowers and Ornaments transforms and guides sentient beings solely through the One Vehicle Dharma;
this is because it is pure, uniform, and unmixed. As for the Buddha King of the Śāla Trees, "Śāla" means "firm" in this language;
his power of vows is firm, providing universal shade for sentient beings like the king of trees. [He is] Jewel Flower Virtue.
The Buddha is characterized by the four virtues of permanence (*nitya*), bliss (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*).

Because the precious flowers have blossomed and do not wither or fall away, one perceives the Buddha of all meanings; for the infinite meanings of all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, are likewise infinite.

yet if one believes but lacks a vow, that belief is not genuine. If one makes a vow but lacks belief, that vow will surely lack steadfastness. Both are [deficient].
This is able to block the path to rebirth [in the realms of suffering]. Therefore, faith and aspiration are used as the concluding summary. This constitutes the fourth layer of exhortation.
From the beginning up to this point, it has repeatedly clarified the making of vows and the seeking of birth in the Pure Land. Now, once again, it clarifies that aspiration arises from faith.
While the three preceding exhortations merely stated that one "should" make a vow, they did not yet manifest the merit of making such a vow. Now...
It is said that whether in the past, future, or present, those who possess a vow will certainly attain rebirth; only then does one realize that the power of the vow is so vast.
How could one not believe this? How could one not make such a vow? Therefore, it is called the fourth exhortation, and is also termed the summary conclusion.

They are able to perform deeds that are exceedingly difficult and rare.
For example, as I now do, by extolling the inconceivable merits of Amitābha Buddha and all other Buddhas;
this clarifies that the Buddhas praise one another to reveal this dharma that is difficult to believe, desiring to cause sentient beings—
It means to give rise to faith within that which is difficult to believe. As for the words "thus it was said," these are the eulogies found below.

*Śākyamuni*: *Śākya* means "Capable One" (*Nengren*); *Muni* means "Silent Sage" (*Jimo*). "An exceedingly difficult and rare matter" refers to attaining *bodhi* in the world of the five turbidities, as described in the passage below;
namely, preaching the Dharma that is difficult to believe for the sake of sentient beings. This is it.

Second, they are able to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within the Sahā world-system, amidst the five turbidities of this evil age: the turbidity of the eon, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of lifespan.
"Saha" means "Endurance," because the sentient beings therein are capable of enduring all manner of suffering.

As for the "evil world of the five turbidities" (*pañca-kaṣāya*), it is called an evil world because the five factors mutually disturb and cloud the true nature. Where these five turbidities do not exist, that is a Pure Land.
Regarding the mutual disturbance by the five factors: although the fundamental nature is originally profound and clear, due to the [five factors] such as the kalpa... [the text continues].
"Defilement (kaṣāya) gives rise to all manner of dust and dregs. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: 'It is like clear water into which sand and soil are thrown;

the soil loses its distinctness and obstruction, the water forfeits its purity, and it becomes turbid and muddy. The meaning of defilement can be understood from this. Regarding the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*):"
This is called the "period" (*kalpa*). An eon (*kalpa*) has no inherently turbid essence; it receives its name because the four turbidities (*kaṣāya*) converge and become intermingled.
As for the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*): "view" refers to the view of a self, extreme views, false views, and so forth. When expanded, there are sixty-two such views.

Because sentient beings possess these various views in abundance, they fall into saṃsāra. As for the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*): "affliction" (*klesa*) means to disturb; "torment" (*nna*) means to...

Harm refers to greed, hatred, ignorance, and so forth, which afflict and injure the mind, causing it to sink into and deviate from its true nature. As for the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*):
by grasping at the retribution of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), views, and pride, these three factors are conventionally designated as "sentient beings.

They falsely establish a sovereign self within form and mind; like sticky glue, they cling and create karma, wandering through the four modes of birth. This is called turbidity. As for the turbidity of lifespan (*āyus-kaṣāya*):...
The breath, warmth, and consciousness—these three are bound together and maintained as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); when even one of them is not maintained, the life-faculty is severed.
As for "turbidity" (*kaṣāya*), it refers to wandering, drifting, and sinking through successive births and lifetimes without a moment’s rest;
thus, to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within such a world of the five turbidities is a difficult feat.
Since the time of Śākyamuni, there has been no second person [to equal him]; this is what makes him rare and extraordinary.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he preaches this Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe.

"All" refers to the aforementioned inconceivable merits and so forth that have been praised, as well as the fact that through hearing this sutra and upholding its name, one is protected by the Buddha and attains rebirth in the Pure Land—all of these are teachings difficult to believe.

How much more so for those who, regardless of whether their faculties are sharp or dull, their vessels pure or defiled, their karma good or evil, or the time long or short, are able to believe and aspire; they shall immediately go and be reborn. This is the Dharma.
It is most rare among the rare, and most difficult to believe among the difficult to believe.

That one is able to preach within this world of the five turbidities and evil ages, causing sentient beings to believe and accept it so that they may attain the path to Bodhi—this is the most difficult among difficulties.
This is why we all join in praising it.
Śāriputra, you should know that in this world of five turbidities, I have performed this difficult task:
having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I preach this dharma so difficult to believe for the sake of all the world. This is truly most difficult.
The words of the Buddhas mentioned in the preceding text are now further clarified and restated.
Truly, these are not the empty praises of the Buddhas; our Buddha has not unworthily received such magnificent acclaim.
As the Sūtra says, "This is extremely difficult," which reveals the earnest intent of our Śākyamuni Buddha as he exhorts sentient beings to believe in this Dharma that is so difficult to believe.

Furthermore, fearing that sentient beings might be unable to have full faith and full aspiration, thereby losing their great benefit, he may be said to have been repeatedly and earnestly exhorting them with a heart of extreme urgency. [The Section on the True Teaching concludes.]
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Śāriputra, all the bhikṣus, and the entire world—including devas, humans, asuras, and others—realized that the Dharma would surely circulate.
This was because the Buddha preached the Dharma for the sake of universally delivering sentient beings so that they might be reborn in the Pure Land. All...
"Bhikṣus" refers to Śāriputra and the great assembly. "Humans and devas" has been explained in the preceding text. "Asuras" means "non-devas";

although their wealth and pleasures are equal to those of the devas, they are called non-devas because they lack divine conduct. There are four types in detail, but fearing prolixity, they are not enumerated here.
Therefore, at the beginning of the sutra it clarifies that the assembly listens to the Dharma, and at the end of the sutra it clarifies that the assembly receives the Dharma.
It is so. From beginning to end, it is perfectly illuminated, lacking nothing and leaving nothing behind. To let go is the Amitābha of one’s own nature;
to raise it up, he is present within a single mote of dust. It is utterly sufficient, a thousandfold and ten-thousandfold.

Such being the text, since Śāriputra has already completed it entirely, what further need is there for Mañjuśrī to strike the gavel or for [the Master] to tap the sounding block at the Twin Trees? Only then can it be called [complete].

The preaching of the Dharma was concluded. As it is said, "Ascending the hall and entering the chamber," the great assembly neither increased; as the drum fell silent and the bell subsided, those among devas and humans did not diminish.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, they received it with joy and faith, paid their respects, and departed.
Regarding "joyful": the meaning has varying depths. Some attain the benefit of joy upon hearing the sutra; others realize the principle and enter the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Therefore, the *Mahāsāṃnipāta-sūtra* concludes by stating that immeasurable sentient beings have resolved their minds on Bodhi, and as many as *nayuta*s of people have done so.
This refers to attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣurviśuddhi*). Although all sūtras contain a conclusion regarding the benefits [of the teaching], this sūtra states:
"You sentient beings, you should all believe and accept my words. Thus, the belief and acceptance at present derive from this sūtra as the means for attaining the essential meaning.
The *Dhāraṇī for Eradicating the Root of All Karmic Obstacles and Attaining Birth in the Pure Land*, as spoken by the Buddha in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
This name of the dhāraṇī was translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. [The name] "Guṇa" consists of five characters.
This is called Guṇabhadra. I shall now briefly explain the name of this mantra. This mantra is found in detail in the *Acintyaprabhāva-avadāna*.
Those who uphold this mantra extinguish their sins and attain rebirth in the Pure Land by uprooting karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*). Generally, there are three types of obstructions:

the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the obstruction of karma, and the obstruction of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). When one speaks merely of "karma," it refers to the middle [obstruction] as a way of encompassing both the initial cause and the subsequent result.
This is an obstruction. Therefore, in removing obstructions, it is vital to remove their root. By now holding this mantra, afflictions will not arise;
this is to uproot the very foundation of karma. As for attaining rebirth in the Pure Land, wandering through the cycle of birth and death in this Sahā world is entirely due to karmic obstructions.
Once the karmic obstructions are emptied and the seeds of the defiled land are extinguished, one will be reborn according to one's vows.
As for *dhāraṇī*, this is translated as "total retention" (*saṃgraha-dhāraṇa*); it encompasses all phenomena and maintains immeasurable meanings. It is the general name for mantras.
Namo Amitābhāya. Tathāgatāya. Tadyathā: Amṛte, dūbhe, amṛte, śāntabhe, amṛte, vikaraṇate, amṛte, vikaraṇade, gamini, gagane, citrakari, svāhā.
The mantras have not been translated since antiquity; they are the secret dharmas of all Buddhas. The sutra is the manifest aspect of the mantra, and the mantra is the esoteric aspect of the sutra.
To uphold both is to possess the dual excellence in its entirety; to recite even one alone still encompasses the other.
This sutra specifically directs one toward the practice of holding the name; even with as few as ten recitations, one attains rebirth. This is the inconceivable vow of Amitābha Buddha.
This is because it is easy to understand. This *Yìjiě* (Easy Explanation) was originally composed for beginners to cultivate the causes for the Pure Land and attain the fruit of Bodhi.
Therefore, the causes are all treated with brevity; thus, while the text is concise and easy to comprehend, its interpretation is difficult. To know its meaning is what constitutes its excellence.

The general principle is this: while the extensive explanations of the Sanskrit terms have been abbreviated and only their names translated, and the numerical categories of dharmas merely indicate their totals, this is intended to enable students to grasp the general outline.
This differs from a formal commentary, which seeks to provide a complete exposition of all aspects.
Nevertheless, there are matters that require clarification and those that require detailed analysis, such as when the sutra speaks of "holding the name" through roots of goodness and merit.
Regarding the Dharma of this practice, the efficacy of rebirth, and the meaning of non-retrogression from Bodhi, these principles must be thoroughly understood.
When the principle is thoroughly understood, faith, aspiration, and practice will converge within a single thought-moment; that is to say, one is three, and three are one.
If this principle is clearly understood, then holding the name will not lead one into the path of Māra. Furthermore, I do not dare allow students to fall into the trap of conceptual speculation.
Although the words and meanings are numerous, the ultimate intent lies solely in the pure cause. It requires nothing more than single-mindedness without distraction;
by reciting the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha," one takes the essence of pure awakening as the cause to shatter all deluded thoughts.
To sever ignorance is to accomplish the pure cause. Therefore, this present easy practice is nothing other than an aid for beginners to engender faith and assist them in holding the name.
